paragraphs.heading: Benzene and its family
paragraphs.text: Benzene, C₆H₆, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon and the first compound to be defined as one. Aromatic compounds turn up all over nature and industry. Benzene, toluene and xylene, known together as BTX, are the key industrial ones. Many molecules in living things carry phenyl groups, among them the aromatic amino acids.

paragraphs.heading: How the benzene ring holds together
paragraphs.text: Joseph Loschmidt and August Kekulé each worked out benzene's bonding in the 19th century. Its carbons form a hexagon, and each carbon has four electrons to share. One goes into a sigma bond with a hydrogen, and one bonds to each of the two neighbouring carbons. The six electrons left over are shared evenly around the whole ring in delocalized pi orbitals as big as the ring itself. That is why all six carbon–carbon bonds are alike, each with a bond order of 1.5.

paragraphs.heading: Electrons above and below
paragraphs.text: The shared electrons are pictured as floating above and below the ring. The fields they create help keep the ring flat. The same equal bonds can also be explained with resonance forms.

paragraphs.heading: The circle symbol
paragraphs.text: Chemists often mark aromaticity with a circle symbol. Robert Robinson and his student James Armit introduced it in 1925, and the Morrison & Boyd organic chemistry textbook made it popular from 1959. How to use it is still argued over: some apply it to any cyclic π system, others only to those that obey Hückel's rule, and some would keep it for single rings with 6 π electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Groups on the ring
paragraphs.text: Benzene derivatives carry from one to six substituents on the ring. Phenol has one hydroxyl group and toluene one methyl group. With two or more, their positions matter, and they are labelled ortho, meta and para. Electron-donating substituents are called activators and steer new groups to the ortho and para positions, while electron-withdrawing deactivators steer them to meta.

paragraphs.heading: Counting the isomers of cresol
paragraphs.text: Cresol shows how this works. Its methyl and hydroxyl groups can sit side by side (ortho), one position apart (meta) or two positions apart (para), so three isomers exist. Both groups are ortho-para directors, so the ortho and para forms are usually favoured. Xylenol adds a second methyl group, and it has 6 isomers.

paragraphs.heading: Aromatic rings beyond benzene
paragraphs.text: Any ring that obeys Hückel's rule without being a benzene derivative can also count as aromatic. One example is the cyclopropenium cation, which meets the rule with n equal to 0. Other rings swap a carbon for a heteroatom such as nitrogen, oxygen or sulfur. Pyridine has a six-membered ring with one nitrogen, pyrrole a five-membered ring with nitrogen, and furan a five-membered ring with one oxygen.

paragraphs.heading: Fused rings
paragraphs.text: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs, are made of fused aromatic rings with no heteroatoms or substituents, and naphthalene is the simplest. They occur in oil, coal and tar, and they form when fossil fuels or biomass burn. Some have been found to be carcinogenic, mutagenic or teratogenic, so they are a concern as pollutants. Meat grilled or barbecued at high heat and smoked fish can hold high levels. In graphene the same fused-ring pattern stretches into large 2D sheets.
